title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 45–46
description: C1–C2 vocabulary and collocations for international development, debt, trade, economic downturns, personal banking, savings and investment.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the user-supplied book. Vocabulary targets are selected from teaching units, exercises and answer-key items; all example sentences and explanatory notes were independently written, and the book’s original exercise passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching sections, definitions, diagrams and usage notes for Units 45 and 46; exercises 45.1–45.4 and 46.1–46.4; and relevant answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Conservative broad British IPA for selected short targets. Longer expressions and items without a sufficiently verified IPA have empty transcriptions; accents and connected speech are not exhaustively represented.
audit.languagePolicy: Learner-facing fields, metadata and notes are in English; Brazilian Portuguese is used only in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared the complete unit teaching and exercise pages with the answer key; reviewed source-target coverage, idiomatic translations, register, collocations, original examples, provenance, word-audio targets, structural fields and identifier uniqueness. Static checks were performed locally.
audit.limitations: No MP3 recordings are bundled. VocabLab browser import, browser TTS and speech recognition have not been tested. Financial examples describe language usage rather than financial advice; terminology may differ by country and banking system.

units.title: Unit 45 — Economy and finance
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 45. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Economy and society · development, debt and trade
learningObjectives: Use collocations to describe sustainable development, growth, poverty and international aid.
Distinguish debt burden, repayment, easing, cancellation and relief.
Discuss trade barriers, sanctions, embargoes and monetary unions precisely.
Describe recessions, currency devaluation and measures to stimulate an economy.

sectionsChecked: A: international aid and development, including collocations and definitions
B: debt collocations and word network
D: economic difficulties and common-mistake box

items.example: The agency aims to support sustainable development rather than short-lived improvements.
items.note: In this unit, sustainable emphasises development that can continue in the long term.

items.pt: criar raízes; começar a se estabelecer
items.example: The programme took root once local organisations became involved.
items.note: Figurative use: become established and begin to succeed; past took root.

items.example: There are encouraging signs that investment is returning to the region.
items.note: Collocates with of recovery or that-clause; describes evidence giving grounds for hope.

items.example: The country achieved economic growth despite difficult trading conditions.
items.note: Achieve economic growth is a common economics collocation.

items.example: Foreign direct investment helped expand the country's manufacturing sector.
items.note: Investment from abroad in business activities or assets; often abbreviated FDI.

items.example: Disruptions at major ports can affect world trade.
items.note: The exchange of goods and services internationally.

items.pt: recuperar-se de uma queda; retomar após um declínio
items.example: Export revenue gradually recovered from a prolonged decline.
items.note: Recover from a decline means improve after a period of falling performance.

items.example: A national economy may expand without every household becoming wealthier.
items.note: Expand describes economic growth; compare expand by a percentage.

items.example: Families facing deep poverty often lack reliable access to essential services.
items.note: Strong collocation; abject poverty is a more emphatic alternative.

items.example: The report describes communities living in abject poverty.
items.note: Emphatic, relatively formal description of severe deprivation.

items.example: The new programme aims to tackle poverty in isolated communities.
items.note: Tackle means make a serious effort to deal with a problem, not necessarily eliminate it.

items.example: The council allocated funds to upgrade rural water supplies.
items.note: Allocate funds to a project or for a purpose.

items.pt: subsídio ou verba concedida para desenvolvimento
items.example: The cooperative received a development grant to improve its facilities.
items.note: Usually a grant that supports development rather than a loan that must be repaid.

items.pt: adotar e implementar uma política; seguir determinada política
items.example: The ministry is pursuing a policy of expanding public transport.
items.note: Pursue and follow a policy are both natural; pursue stresses active implementation.

items.pt: seguir uma política; adotar determinada linha de ação
items.example: The organisation followed a policy of publishing its financial accounts.
items.note: Follow a policy emphasises acting consistently with it; an alternative to pursue a policy.

items.example: Leaders pledged to eradicate poverty, although progress has been uneven.
items.note: Eradicate means remove completely, stronger than reduce or tackle.

items.pt: ampliar ou melhorar o acesso a
items.example: Investment in transport can improve access to schools and hospitals.
items.note: The preposition is to: access to healthcare, education or clean water.

items.example: The company incurred debt to finance the construction of a new plant.
items.note: Formal collocation: incur debt, losses or costs; past incurred.

items.example: It may take the council years to repay its debt.
items.note: Repay debt means pay back money owed; not simply pay for a purchase.

items.pt: peso da dívida; ônus do endividamento
items.example: High interest rates have increased the debt burden on small businesses.
items.note: Refers to the financial pressure caused by debt obligations.

items.example: A debtor country may negotiate new repayment terms with its creditors.
items.note: A nation that owes money; compare creditor country, which lends money.

items.example: Debt restructuring could ease the debt burden on poorer nations.
items.note: Easing reduces the pressure of debt without necessarily cancelling the amount owed.

items.pt: aliviar o endividamento; reduzir o peso da dívida
items.example: International agreements may help alleviate debt in countries facing a crisis.
items.note: Formal alternative to ease debt or ease the debt burden.

items.example: The lenders agreed to cancel part of the country's debt.
items.note: Cancel debt means remove an obligation to repay; stronger than reschedule it.

items.pt: alívio da dívida; medidas de redução ou perdão de dívidas
items.example: The aid package included debt relief for struggling governments.
items.note: Can include reducing, rescheduling or forgiving debt, depending on the programme.

items.example: The two governments negotiated a free trade agreement covering agricultural products.
items.note: Agreement intended to reduce barriers to trade between participating countries.

items.pt: disputa comercial; controvérsia entre parceiros comerciais
items.example: The trade dispute delayed the shipment of several important goods.
items.note: A disagreement about trade policy, restrictions or market access.

items.pt: práticas restritivas ao comércio ou à concorrência
items.example: Regulators investigated restrictive practices that limited access to the market.
items.note: Practices that hinder free trade or competition; the precise legal meaning varies.

items.example: The trade war led both sides to raise tariffs on imported goods.
items.note: Economic retaliation between trading partners, rather than armed warfare.

items.example: The regional bloc decided to impose sanctions on the government.
items.note: Sanctions are imposed on a country or organisation; their form and scope may vary.

items.example: Negotiators discussed when to lift sanctions following the agreement.
items.note: Lift means officially remove restrictions previously imposed.

items.example: The embargo restricted exports of several industrial products.
items.note: An embargo prohibits or severely restricts trade in specified goods or with a particular country.

items.example: Exporters resumed business after the authorities lifted the embargo.
items.note: Common verb for ending an embargo; impose an embargo is its opposite.

items.example: The proposed monetary union would require closer coordination of financial policy.
items.note: An arrangement linking countries through shared monetary institutions or a currency.

items.example: The members debated whether adopting a single currency would benefit trade.
items.note: A common currency used by more than one country in a monetary union.

items.example: Rebuilding a war-torn economy requires infrastructure and stable institutions.
items.note: War-torn describes the severe effects of prolonged armed conflict.

items.example: The government announced emergency support for the ailing economy.
items.note: Ailing is figurative here: weak or experiencing serious difficulties.

items.example: The central bank chose not to devalue the currency during the crisis.
items.note: To lower a currency's official value relative to other currencies; not devaluate.

items.example: The sudden devaluation made imported machinery more expensive.
items.note: Noun from devalue, commonly used for official reductions in currency value.

items.example: Authorities decided to revalue the currency after sustained economic growth.
items.note: Revalue is the opposite of devalue in the source's currency context.

items.example: A currency revaluation can make imported goods cheaper in local terms.
items.note: An upward adjustment in a currency's value relative to others.

items.example: Analysts warned that the country might go into recession next year.
items.note: Common collocation for the beginning of an economic recession.

items.example: The economy emerged from recession after investment began to recover.
items.note: Means return to economic expansion after recession.

items.pt: recessão em duas quedas; recessão com breve recuperação intermediária
items.example: The region experienced a double-dip recession when output fell again after a brief recovery.
items.note: A recession followed by temporary improvement and another downturn.

items.example: Farmers struggled after a slump in prices for their crops.
items.note: Slump is a sharp, serious fall; often a slump in commodity or house prices.

items.example: Investment in transport was intended to boost the economy.
items.note: Boost means stimulate growth or activity; it does not guarantee long-term recovery.

units.title: Unit 46 — Personal finance: making ends meet
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 46. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Personal finance · banking, expenses and investments
learningObjectives: Choose between informal and more formal expressions for financial hardship and payments.
Use accurate British-English vocabulary for banking, payment cards and transfers.
Explain everyday terms for savings, compensation, investment and inherited money.
Recognise collocations for borrowing, debt and basic financial risk.

sectionsChecked: A: cash, cheques and cards, with register and banking glosses
B: savings, pensions and investment text boxes with numbered definitions

items.example: I can't go out tonight because I'm completely broke.
items.note: Informal predicative adjective meaning you have no money available; not the same as bankrupt.

items.example: By the end of the festival, everyone in our group was skint.
items.note: Very informal British English, similar to broke but colloquial in register.

items.pt: nadando em dinheiro; cheio de grana
items.example: Since selling his business, he seems to be rolling in it.
items.note: Informal idiom meaning having a great deal of money; it does not literally refer to rolling.

items.pt: conseguir pagar as contas; fazer o dinheiro chegar ao fim do mês
items.example: Rising rent has made it harder for some families to make ends meet.
items.note: Means manage essential living costs with available income.

items.pt: a situação financeira está apertada; o dinheiro está curto
items.example: We are postponing the holiday because things are tight this year.
items.note: Informal expression referring to limited money, not physical tightness.

items.pt: com pouco dinheiro disponível; apertado de grana
items.example: The business was strapped for cash while waiting for a major customer to pay.
items.note: Informal phrase for a shortage of available money; commonly be strapped for cash.

items.example: The couple was deeply in debt after several unexpected expenses.
items.note: Deeply in debt describes serious indebtedness, not just a temporary shortage of cash.

items.pt: um cheque é devolvido por falta de fundos ou recusa bancária
items.example: The supplier complained when the cheque bounced for the second time.
items.note: Informal banking verb; a bank refuses to honour the cheque, for example due to insufficient funds.

items.pt: preencher um cheque em nome de
items.example: Please make the cheque out to the community association.
items.note: The payee's name follows to; slightly less formal than make it payable to.
items.speechText: make a cheque out to the charity

items.pt: emitir cheque nominal a; preencher cheque em favor de
items.example: Make the cheque payable to the university rather than the individual lecturer.
items.note: More formal alternative to make a cheque out to someone.
items.speechText: make a cheque payable to the charity

items.example: The membership fee is collected by direct debit every month.
items.note: A pre-authorised payment collection from a bank account, often recurring; UK-oriented banking term.

items.example: The charity received the donation by electronic transfer.
items.note: Money moved electronically between accounts; distinct from a scheduled direct debit.

items.word: put it on a credit card
items.pt: lançar a compra no cartão de crédito
items.example: Shall we put it on a credit card and split the bill later?
items.note: Informal phrasing for charging a purchase to a credit card; it refers to the purchase, not the card itself.

items.word: stick it on a credit card
items.pt: colocar a compra no cartão de crédito
items.example: We didn't have cash, so we stuck it on a credit card.
items.note: Very informal alternative to put it on a credit card.

items.word: charge it to a credit card
items.pt: cobrar a compra no cartão de crédito
items.example: Could you charge it to my credit card instead of taking cash?
items.note: More formal or service-oriented than stick it on a card.

items.pt: taxa percentual anual; taxa anual de juros efetiva divulgada
items.example: The APR on the loan was higher than the advertised introductory rate.
items.note: Annual percentage rate; its exact composition is regulated differently across markets.

items.example: Please check the card expiry date before completing the payment.
items.note: British English expiry date; also an expiration date in American usage.

items.pt: um cartão vence; perde a validade
items.example: Her debit card expires next month, so she requested a replacement.
items.note: Expires in a given month or on a date means ceases to be valid.

items.example: The bank alerted customers to an increase in credit card fraud.
items.note: Criminal misuse of card details or a credit card account.

items.example: I prefer a debit card because the payment comes directly from my bank account.
items.note: Uses money from an associated account rather than normal credit borrowing.

items.pt: cartão de loja; cartão de crédito de uma rede varejista
items.example: The shop offered a discount to customers using its store card.
items.note: A card issued by a retailer, often offering credit or benefits restricted to that retailer.

items.example: She went to the bank to withdraw money for the trip.
items.note: More formal than get money out; withdraw money from a bank account.

items.pt: sacar dinheiro; tirar dinheiro da conta
items.example: I'll get some money out before we reach the market.
items.note: Informal British English alternative to withdraw money, especially at a cash machine.

items.pt: senha numérica pessoal; número de identificação pessoal
items.example: He entered his PIN incorrectly at the payment terminal.
items.note: Personal identification number; PIN is pronounced like the word pin, so PIN number is redundant.

items.example: The nearest ATM is inside the railway station.
items.note: Automated teller machine; normally pronounced as separate letters.

items.example: There is a cashpoint next to the supermarket entrance.
items.note: Common British English term for an ATM; originally a branded name.

items.example: The bus accepts payments made with a contactless card.
items.note: A card that can pay by tapping, without inserting it into a reader.

items.example: Contactless payment has become standard at many railway stations.
items.note: Payment made through near-field technologies using a card or compatible device.

items.pt: quantia paga de uma só vez; montante único
items.example: The insurance company offered a lump sum instead of monthly payments.
items.note: A single payment rather than instalments; often lump-sum payment before a noun.

items.example: Residents received compensation payments after the construction delays.
items.note: Money paid to compensate for loss, injury or damage.

items.pt: indenização generosa pela saída de um cargo; pacote de desligamento
items.example: The departing executive negotiated a substantial golden handshake.
items.note: Often a large payment on leaving a senior job; not a regular handshake or bonus.

items.example: Staff may receive an annual bonus if the organisation meets its targets.
items.note: Additional payment generally made once a year, often linked to performance.

items.pt: carteira de ações; conjunto de investimentos em ações
items.example: She diversified her share portfolio across several industries.
items.note: British English for a set of investments in company shares.

items.pt: mercado de ações; bolsa de valores em sentido amplo
items.example: The stock market fell sharply after the unexpected announcement.
items.note: Market where company shares are bought and sold; does not mean a physical shop.

items.pt: ações e títulos de participação em empresas
items.example: The adviser explained the risks of investing in stocks and shares.
items.note: Conventional British English binomial for equity investments; the precise terminology varies.

items.pt: economias de uma vida; todas as economias acumuladas
items.example: He lost much of his life savings in a fraudulent scheme.
items.note: Savings built up over a long period; normally plural savings.

items.example: She updated her will after the birth of her daughter.
items.note: Legal document stating how assets should be distributed after death; rules vary by jurisdiction.

items.example: He decided to leave money in his will to a local charity.
items.note: To leave someone money or property in a will means bequeath it.

items.pt: cobrir o custo; ter valor suficiente para pagar
items.example: The grant was not enough to cover the cost of all the repairs.
items.note: Cover a cost means be sufficient to pay it.

items.pt: tomar muito dinheiro emprestado; contrair grandes empréstimos
items.example: The firm borrowed heavily to fund its rapid expansion.
items.note: Refers to borrowing a large amount; borrow from a lender, not lend from.

items.example: We borrowed from the bank rather than from relatives.
items.note: Borrow from someone is the opposite perspective from lend to someone.

items.pt: roubo de identidade; uso indevido dos dados pessoais
items.example: Identity theft may involve someone opening an account using stolen details.
items.note: Related to card fraud but broader; included as an alternative in the exercise answer key.
